Skip next section Ukraine civilian casualties hit highest level since 2022 08/13/2026 August 13, 2026 Ukraine civilian casualties hit highest level since 2022 Civilian casualties in Ukraine have climbed to their highest monthly level since the early weeks of Russia's full-scale invasion, according to the United Nations. The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine said it verified at least 437 civilians killed and 2,610 injured in July, a 30% rise from June and 70% more than in July 2025. July recorded the highest overall number of civilian casualties since March 2022, while the number of people killed was the highest since May 2022. The UN said the true toll was likely higher, with some reports still being verified. Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022, the UN has verified at least 16,874 civilian deaths and 51,273 injuries in Ukraine. Long-range missiles and drones remained the biggest cause of civilian casualties in July, accounting for 38% of the total. Short-range drones operating close to the frontline accounted for another 27% of casualties. “Civilians are facing intensified risks from the increased use of missiles and drones in urban centers, glide bombs in cities closer to the frontline, and short-range drones," said head of the mission Danielle Bell. Russia launched at least 429 missiles during the month, more than twice the number fired in June, according to the UN. The deadliest attack came on July 2, when Russian forces launched 74 missiles and almost 500 long-range drones, mostly against Kyiv. At least 30 civilians were killed and 104 injured. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said 340 people were on board when a drone struck and destroyed the locomotive. Zelenskyy said the locomotive driver and his assistant were killed in the attack. None of the passengers was injured, according to the head of Ukraine's state railway operator. Footage released by emergency services showed flames engulfing the damaged front of the train. Zelenskyy accused the drone operator of knowingly targeting a civilian train, saying it would have been impossible not to recognize the nature of the target. Russian forces have repeatedly struck Ukraine's railway network during the war, hitting trains, stations and other infrastructure. Kyiv says the attacks are intended both to disrupt transport and logistics and to target civilian life. Zelenskyy said Russian forces had also launched more than 130 attack drones overnight, with strikes reported across 11 regions. He again called for additional air defenses and stronger international pressure on Moscow. https://p.dw.com/p/5IknM Skip next section Welcome to our coverage Published 08/13/2026 Published August 13, 2026 last updated 08/13/2026 last updated August 13, 2026 Welcome to our coverage Richard Connor | Louis Oelofse Editor The United Nations says civilian casualties in July reached their highest monthly level since the early weeks of the full-scale invasion. http://www.parisguardian.com/news/279242.text: Britains forgotten proxy war against Russia RT.com 14 Aug 2026, 22:11 GMT+10 London armed Russias enemies, promised them independence, and walked away when its imperial gamble collapsed What is there in common between Ukrainians and the highlanders of the Caucasus, and what parallels can be drawn between Russia and Great Britain in the 19th century, and these same countries in the 21st century? In the 19th century, the British Empire fought against the Russian Empire using the highlanders in the Caucasus in a way that's very similar to how Britain is now using Ukrainians. In the 19th century, the Russian and British empires clashed fiercely over spheres of influence in the Caucasus. This geopolitical rivalry made use of all the means available at the time: wars between spies and diplomats, covert operations, arms smuggling, ideological battles, and active media propaganda. Read more about the confrontation between Russia and Britain, the secret operations in the Caucasus, and the lessons that those who now place their trust in Britain should draw from history. To India via the Caucasus "Britain will defend the freedom-loving nation from Russian aggression," "British military advisers supplied fighters with weapons to resist the Russian army," "British diplomats organized elites to combat Russian influence" - such headlines have become commonplace in Western media during the Ukraine conflict. Yet these same phrases could very well describe another historical conflict where British and Russian interests collided: the covert war waged by the British Empire against Russia in the 19th century, aimed at undermining Russian influence in the Caucasus. At first glance, it might seem odd that events in the Caucasus, occurring far from Britain, could threaten London's interests. But it only appears so. After the Napoleonic Wars, the Russian Empire was at the height of its power. It led the "Holy Alliance" - a coalition of European great powers that shaped continental politics. Additionally, during the late 18th and early 19th centuries, Russia achieved significant victories over the Ottoman Empire in several wars, acquiring territories such as New Russia, Crimea, and parts of the eastern Black Sea coast. Naturally, Russia also paid attention to what was happening in the Caucasus. The peoples of the North and West Caucasus, the Circassians, carried out frequent raids on Russian settlers, whom they robbed and enslaved, which caused great concern in Russia. To protect its interests and secure the safety of its people, Russia advanced further into this mountainous territory. Britain, however, perceived this as a direct threat to its interests in India. London believed that Russia wouldn't stop in the Caucasus but would advance further, potentially threatening Persia. And through Persia, and then Afghanistan, there lay a direct path to India, which was then referred to as the "jewel in the crown" of the British Empire. Although there was no concrete evidence that Russia intended to seize distant India, British elites firmly held this belief. In order to safeguard India against the mythical "Russian threat," Britain encouraged tensions in the Caucasus. In service of the Crown Britain's active intervention in Russian affairs in the Caucasus was preceded by two wars: the Russo-Persian War of 1826-1828 and the Russo-Turkish War of 1828-1829. As a result of these military triumphs, Russia solidified its position in Transcaucasia and gained control over much of the eastern coastline of the Black Sea. Fearing Russia's growing power in the region, Britain started supplying the Circassians with weapons and ammunition as early as 1830. For instance, in December of that year, six weapon-laden vessels were intercepted off the coast of what is now Abkhazia. However, for a time, these arms shipments remained limited to smuggling. A turning point in Russia-Britain relations came with the arrival of British diplomat David Urquhart in Istanbul. A highly energetic individual, Urquhart had joined the rebels who fought for Greek independence when he was just 16 years old. After the war, he stayed in the region and developed a keen interest in the politics and culture of the Ottoman Empire. By 1833, he was appointed to the British trade delegation in Istanbul, and in 1835 he became the embassy secretary. It was Urquhart who crafted Britain's aggressive anti-Russia policy in the Caucasus. David Urquhart Creative Commons CC by NC Urquhart initiated the work of British diplomats and spies directly in Circassia, as the Northern and Western Caucasus regions were then called. He attended elder councils and fervently promoted the idea of waging war against Russia. Notably, he was behind the adoption of a "national oath" by the mountain peoples, proposing that the Circassians unite for a common cause against Russia instead of fighting each other. He also persuaded the Circassians to take an oath according to which anyone who entered negotiations with the Russians would be killed, their possessions divided among their executioners, and their families sold into slavery. A parallel can be drawn with contemporary Ukrainian politics, where any possibility of peacefully resolving the conflict with Russia is utterly unacceptable, and proponents of such initiatives face severe repercussions. Urquhart proved to be an effective diplomat and spy, convincing Circassian leaders that Britain genuinely sought their independence. In reality, they were merely pawns in the hands of British agents, sacrificing themselves in the name of the British Empire, which was only concerned about the illusory Russian threat in India. Britain also supplied the highlanders with arms. British intelligence agents James Bell and James Longworth oversaw smuggling operations that delivered firearms to the Caucasus, bribing tribal leaders and elders in the region. For an extended period, they lived undercover in the Caucasus, adopting Muslim names and fictitious titles. On behalf of the British government, they promised the Circassians that Britain was committed to protecting their independence and even vowed to fight against Russia. Throughout the 1830s, dozens of British agents were active in the Caucasus. Most importantly, Urquhart focused on a propaganda war. An ardent Russophobe, he convinced the British public that Russia posed a deadly existential threat to the British Empire. He argued that Russia was preparing to conquer Persia and further invade India. The British press played a crucial role in spreading fears of a "Russian threat." Newspapers reported on the struggle of the "freedom-loving highlanders" against the "barbaric Russian oppressors." They conveniently overlooked the fact that the highlanders themselves were quite savage at the time - slave trade and blood feuds were common in the region, and the enlightened Russian Empire resolutely opposed this. But just like in Ukraine today, the London media exaggerated the losses of the Russian Army, insisting that the decisive support of the highlanders would ensure Russia's defeat in the Caucasus. The 'Vixen' case While Britain's supply of weapons to the highlanders and its organizational and ideological efforts harmed Russia, this did not decisively influence the course of the conflict. British hawks opted for provocation, aiming to ignite a conflict between Russia and Britain and other Western European nations. The pretext they found was rather unusual. Schooner 'Vixen', 1853 Wikimedia / Art UK / Public domain Russia was defending its legitimate interests in the Caucasus and sought to halt arms shipments to the highlanders. To this end, the Russian Navy patrolled the eastern Black Sea coast, directing all foreign commercial vessels to only two ports: Anapa and Redoubt Kali (near modern-day Poti). Britain viewed this as a violation of free trade and resorted to blatant provocation. In November 1836, Russian military brig the Ayaks detained British schooner the Vixen in the port of Sujuk-Qale (modern-day Novorossiysk). The British vessel was unloading arms intended for the highlanders: eight cannons, nearly 13 tons of gunpowder, and a large quantity of firearms. Clearly, this wasn't about free trade; this was direct military support for Russia's adversaries. The expedition was organized by none other than Urquhart, while the captain of the schooner was the British spy Bell. Remarkably, Bell didn't hide his intentions; he openly sought to provoke the Russian fleet. After the capture, the Vixen was confiscated, and its crew expelled to Türkiye. This incident sparked a major scandal that nearly brought the Russian and British empires to the brink of war. Conservatives in the British Parliament called for the navy to be sent to the Black Sea to confront Russia and questioned the legality of annexing Circassia. However, the British radicals miscalculated. Russian Emperor Nicholas I refused to back down. Instead, he placed the armed forces on heightened alert and demonstrated an unwavering commitment to defending Russia's interests in the Caucasus. No one in Europe was willing to wage war against Russia either. As a result, London had to recall Urquhart from Istanbul and abandon all its demands regarding Russian influence in the Caucasus. Not just the Crimean War The war in the Caucasus could have concluded as early as the late 1830s. However, the British weren't ready to accept defeat and began preparing for another conflict. Agitators infiltrated the eastern Caucasus, modern-day Chechnya and Dagestan, inciting the highlanders to resist Russia. British agents assured them that London would support a rebellion against Russia and provide the necessary weapons and supplies. The strategy was based on the assumption that Russia would become bogged down in the Caucasus and unable to counter British actions elsewhere. And that's indeed what happened. When the Crimean War broke out from 1853 to 1856, 270,000 Russian troops were stationed in the Caucasus to maintain order in the region. Simultaneously with the onset of the Crimean War, attacks on Russian settlements intensified, led by the forces of Imam Shamil, who controlled territories in Chechnya and Dagestan. In the North Caucasus, the Circassians launched assaults on Novorossiysk and Yekaterinodar (modern-day Krasnodar). While these raids had little impact on the overall course of battles, they undoubtedly diverted the focus and resources of the Russian command. A Circassian of the Kabardian Tribe, 1831. Wikimedia / Filippo Pistrucc / Public domain Throughout the Crimean War, the British press frequently raised the issue of "Circassian independence." At the Paris Conference, London also highlighted the Circassian question, demanding that Russia recognize Circassia's independence or, at the very least, withdraw troops from the Caucasus; in exchange London would prevent the highlanders from attacking Russian territories. Despite this diplomatic pressure, the Russian Empire successfully defended its rights in the Caucasus. The likely reason lies in the fact that after more than 20 years of fierce struggle against Russia, the highlanders didn't achieve any considerable progress. As for Russia, even amid a brutal war with the leading European powers of the time, it managed to retain control over the Caucasus. Last attempt Although the Crimean War ended in defeat for the Russian Empire, its position in the Caucasus remained stable. In an attempt to undermine Russia and lay the groundwork for future operations, the British dispatched a group of insurgents to the region in 1857. The contingent was led by Polish military officer Teofil Lapinski, who participated in the 1848 uprising and fought against the Austrians in modern-day Ukraine and Hungary. During the Crimean War, Lapinski fought against Russia while serving in the Polish Corps, which was part of the Ottoman Army. When, after the Crimean War, it became clear that Circassia had no chance of achieving independence, Lapinski began planning a military operation in the area. His mission was financed by pro-British General Zamojski and the Circassian elites that had settled in the Ottoman Empire. The intellectual driving force behind this operation was Stratford de Redcliffe, the British ambassador in Istanbul. Leveraging his considerable influence at the Sultan's court, he secured the support of Ottoman officials and supplied the group with arms and ammunition. Russian envoy Apollinary Butenev managed to uncover the plot and alerted the governor of the Caucasus, Prince Baryatinsky. Nevertheless, British steamship the Kangaroo, commanded by Captain Neggs, eluded Russian cruisers, and in February 1857, the insurgents landed in Tuapse. The core of the unit consisted of Polish soldiers, but it also included Austrian artillerymen, Hungarian mine specialists, and Turkish instructors. British agents provided organizational and intelligence support to Lapinski's group. The insurgent unit was bolstered by defectors from the Russian Army, primarily Poles and Ukrainians, increasing its numbers to around 800 fighters. For about a year and a half, supported by the Circassian nobility, Lapinski effectively resisted the Russian Army. He skillfully utilized the terrain and was supported by the British and Turks. However, General Philipson, who commanded Russian forces in this part of the Caucasus, successfully recruited one of Lapinski's associates, who relayed crucial information about Lapinski's actions to the imperial troops. During a bold Russian naval landing in Gelendzhik, Lapinski narrowly escaped capture. Additionally, the Russians managed to cut off supply lines for weapons and reinforcements to Lapinski's forces and, having gathered reserves, inflicted several painful defeats on the insurgents. Imam Shamil Fine Art Images / Heritage Images / Getty Images The situation worsened when the British realized the inevitable defeat of the Circassians and their insurgent allies and withdrew their support. By the end of 1859, Lapinski and what remained of his insurgent group retreated to Istanbul. That same year, Russian troops captured Imam Shamil, the leader of the highland peoples of the Northeast Caucasus. Though some scattered groups continued to resist, the overall campaign was over. Hundreds of thousands of Circassians unwilling to live under Russian rule relocated to the Ottoman Empire. By 1864, the Caucasian War concluded with Russia's victory, solidifying its control over the region. This triumph not only marked a significant military achievement but also ushered in a lasting peace, the abolition of slavery and brutal traditions, and the beginning of civil governance, education, and economic development in the Caucasus. It was also a triumph for Russia over Britain, which, despite all its diplomacy, intelligence efforts, and covert operations, failed to overcome the strength of Russian intelligence services, diplomacy, and army. This serves as an important reminder to the nations and states that count on the support of Britain when waging war against Russia. While they may have some occasional success, ultimately, the outcome will always be the same. Judges scored the contest 117-110, 114-113 and 114-113 in favor of Knyba, who extended his professional record to 18 wins against one defeat. Ruiz endured a particularly challenging seventh round, during which he was knocked down and only narrowly escaped a stoppage when the bell rang after he scrambled back to his feet. The 36-year-old Mexican-American, who secured a stunning victory over Britain’s Anthony Joshua to claim world titles seven years ago, was taking part in only his fourth bout since losing the rematch to Joshua in December 2019. His career has since been hampered by injuries and prolonged inactivity, with Saturday’s contest marking his first fight since a draw against Jarrell Miller in August 2024. Despite the clear defeat on the scorecards, Ruiz was quick to advocate for an immediate rematch. He attributed much of his struggles to Knyba’s physical style, particularly the Pole’s frequent clinching, which he felt neutralized his offense. “I don’t know, I think it was just him holding,” Ruiz said. “Every time I tried to come in, he’d hold me really tight, and I just couldn’t let my combinations go. He played a good game plan, but I’d love to run it back and do things a lot different.” RELATED NEWS Handball: Nigeria Beat Guinea, Qualify For 2027 IHF Men’s U21 World Championship Ballon d’Or 2026: Ronaldo, Salah, Osimhen, Raphinha Snubs Spark Fan Fury Inter Milan Interest Puts Fulham On Alert Over Super Eagles Star Bassey Ruiz, who recently signed with British promoter Eddie Hearn, dismissed any notion of retirement, instead pointing to a lack of ring time as the primary factor in his performance. He insisted that facing a formidable opponent like Knyba was a calculated risk rather than a misstep. “It was just a long layoff, and it was a great opponent,” Ruiz argued. “I didn’t want to take an easy fight, so that’s why I took Damian. He’s a big guy. But we’ve got to take risks. I’ve still got it in me, man. I’ve just got to stay active and I want to fight again.” We’ve got the edge. Europe Hungarian Money Stops Flowing to Brussels’ Last Conservative Think Tank Hungary’s new government is dismantling conservative institutions built under Orbán, under new leader Peter Magyar’s ‘Operation Purgatory.’ Save Mark Us Preferred on Google Print Frank Furedi, executive director of MCC Brussels, delivers a lecture in Brussels, in this undated image. Courtesy of MCC Brussels Owen Evans 9/25/2026 | Updated: 9/25/2026 0:00 X 1 Just four years after it opened, think tank MCC Brussels, a thorn in the side of the EU’s progressive establishment, has closed after Hungary’s new government cut off the money that kept it running. The office, set up in 2022 as the Brussels outpost of former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán’s linked Mathias Corvinus Collegium, aimed to give national-conservative ideas a home in a city dominated by EU institutions and left-leaning advocacy groups. However, now, its executive director has resigned, staff have gone without salaries, and the organization says its activities have effectively been paralyzed. So what happened? ‘No Dialogue’ MCC Brussels Professor Frank Furedi resigned with immediate effect on Aug. 31, citing the “persistent failure to provide the contractually agreed funds.” “Well, we saw this would be coming. There was no doubt about it,” Furedi told The Epoch Times. Related Stories Hungary Moves to Revoke Orban Ban on Promoting Gender Ideology to Children Hungary’s Parliament Passes Bill to Remove President in Purge of Orban Power Base “But what I never expected was that they would behave in such unprofessional manners. So basically, there was no dialogue. “Our emails were never answered.” He said employees had gone without pay for July and August. “They have families, their rents to pay, and everything else,” he said. In parts of the EU establishment, Orbán was seen as an illiberal disruptor of the bloc, who repeatedly clashed with Brussels over immigration, LGBT policy, Ukraine , and its veto powers, resulting in billions of EU funds being frozen . However, Péter Magyar’s Tisza Party won Hungary’s April election, ending Orbán’s long period in power, and quickly moved against the system of public-interest foundations created during his era, including the foundation behind MCC Brussels. Then-Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán speaks at the press conference during a heads of state meeting of the Visegrad group at the International Congress Center in Katowice, Poland, on June 30, 2021. Omar Marques/Getty Images ‘Operation Purgatory’ Magyar called the drive “Operation Purgatory.” “The state will not finance these things—neither the event called CPAC, nor the Mathias Corvinus Collegium and other affiliated institutions. I say it should not have financed them until now. This was a crime,” Magyar said at the day of his election win press conference on April 12, as reported by Euronews. MCC Brussels was legally a Belgian nonprofit, with Viktor Orbán’s former political director Balázs Orbán, no relation, as its board chairman. It was funded almost entirely by a grant from Mathias Corvinus Collegium’s foundation in Budapest. In 2024, the Brussels office had a budget of about 6.37 million euros ($7.25 million). Nearly all of that came from the Hungarian foundation. That foundation became state-backed in 2020, when the Orbán government put public assets into it, including 10 percent of oil company MOL and 10 percent of drugmaker Gedeon Richter. But Richard Schenk, a MCC Brussels research fellow, told The Epoch Times that the structure left the operation dependent on a single source of funding. “This was by Hungarian law a single source of income,” Schenk said. “Also it came with a lot of restrictions on how to spend this money.” He said that [Victor] Orbán wanted these big subjects debated because of “his experiences of communism in the 1990s.” “He had this experience that you can win government without being actually in power if you don’t have support from outside institutions,” Schenk said. ‘Mission Creeps’ Its investigations looked into how Brussels funds civil-society groups that the think tank said helped shape EU policy. Furedi said even their opponents “recognized that we’re probably the most influential political think tank in Brussels.” “We were able to, for the first time, create a viable, coherent, and appealing conservative intellectual alternative to our political opponents,” he said. Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar addresses the media at EU headquarters in Brussels, on May 29, 2026. Virginia Mayo/AP Photo One report last year, “Mission Creeps,” claimed that at least 220 million euros ($251 million) in EU funding had gone over the previous decade to projects involving NGOs promoting gender ideology. Report author Ashley Frawley told The Epoch Times at the time that activists had played a direct role in drafting EU policies by “radically” redefining gender. A European Commission spokesman said at the time the funding was “provided in full transparency and in line with the Financial Regulation.” A 2024 report looked at how the EU relies on officially designated fact-checkers, some of them NGOs, who flag content for platforms to review and take down. Norman Lewis, a visiting research fellow at MCC Brussels, former PwC director, and former director of technology research at Orange UK, told The Epoch Times at the time that the fact-checkers were not accountable to anyone. “In the end, the commission can claim they’re not censoring but Big Tech is, despite the fact that the commission created the environment that forces this censorship,” he said. Commission spokesman Thomas Regnier said at the time that fact-checkers in the EU work on the basis of “high ethical and professional standards, which guarantee their independence.” In June, the EU Transparency Register, a public database that lists organizations seeking to influence EU law-making and policy, suspended MCC Brussels after a complaint by nonprofit research and campaign group Corporate Europe Observatory. MCC rejected claims that it had failed to cooperate. A spokesman for Corporate Europe Observatory, which is funded by private foundations including the Open Society Foundations, the Sigrid Rausing Trust, Adessium Foundation, and Luminate, accused MCC Brussels of a “far-right witch hunt” against NGOs and their funding, in an email to The Epoch Times. ‘Run Us Out of Town’ Furedi rejected the “far right” label. “People use it as a way of trying to marginalize your voice so that people don’t take it very seriously,” he said. He said MCC had faced hostility from parts of the Brussels political establishment. “They basically did everything possible to isolate us and try to run us out of town,” he said. Antifa’s website, he added, said that MCC Brussels was “the biggest danger to civilization in Brussels.” ‘Looking for a Post-Liberal Alternative’ Under Orbán, Hungary became a draw for American conservatives looking beyond the traditional Republican establishment. MCC Feszt, the foundations’ festival, brought international figures including Peter Thiel and Christopher Rufo to Hungary. Rod Dreher, an American writer who spent several years living in Budapest, said that Hungary had become “a beacon” for what he called “alternative American conservatives.” “Those who were not conventional Republican Party types, but who were looking for a post-liberal alternative,” he told The Epoch Times at the sidelines of the Alliance for Responsible Citizenship (ARC) conference in London in June. Rod Dreher, author of "Live Not by Lies" and a senior editor at The American Conservative, in New York on Jan. 21, 2022. Samira Bouaou/The Epoch Times Dreher said he first went to Hungary in 2019 while researching his book “Live Not By Lies” to learn what lessons people who grew up under communism had to teach others about resisting the “dictatorship of wokeness.” “And I thought this is a normal country,” he said. In 2021, Tucker Carlson spent a week broadcasting from Budapest, which Dreher said changed how MAGA-leaning Americans saw the country. “The Hungarian government was funding that. This was public diplomacy because they had to get their story out somewhere, and so it really did become a sort of haven,” Dreher said. New Think Tank Launched Furedi sees the shutdown of MCC Brussels as more than a policy shift. “There was and still is an atmosphere of not just political differences being acted out, but of vengeance,” he said, adding that he believed that Magyar regarded MCC Brussels as “an enemy that had to be crushed.” He said that he believed there was a “certain synergy” between the new Hungarian government and parts of the European Commission. He added that EU officials had signaled to Hungary that restoring access to EU funding withheld during the Orbán years required the new government to “clean up” Hungary’s political institutions. The Epoch Times could not independently verify that claim. The ​European Commission said on Sept. 23 that ‌it had proposed unlocking 4.2 billion euros ($4.8 billion) in cohesion funds for Hungary. Furedi said the ideas behind MCC Brussels will not necessarily disappear with the institution. On Sept. 22, he and much of the old MCC Brussels team launched Freedom and Sovereignty Initiative Europe, or FSI Europe, a new Belgian nonprofit that says it will argue for a Europe of sovereign nation-states and back what it calls the “patriotic movement” with research and media. “Instead of regarding the situation that we’re in as just simply a setback or a defeat, I look upon it as an opportunity to build a new kind of organization that tries to mobilize political and financial support from people who genuinely believe in a kind of radical conservative project that we’re trying to undertake,” Furedi said. The Epoch Times asked the Hungarian government whether the dismantling of MCC and other Orbán-era foundations was politically motivated, why operational funding was withheld despite leaving Brussels staff unpaid, and whether Hungary still sees itself as a center of European conservatism. The government did not respond. Reuters contributed to this report.
